findings.source_passage: She remained for some minutes gazing after him. Then she gave a curious movement of her shoulders, rather as a terrier shakes himself.
findings.source_locator: After Whittington walks away, before Tuppence's monologue
findings.why_it_matters: The simile 'rather as a terrier shakes himself' is a precise, voice-establishing character image; it conveys Tuppence's instinctive self-possession in a way the draft's bare 'terrier-like shake' diminishes.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full simile: 'gave a curious movement of her shoulders, rather as a terrier shakes himself' rather than the compressed 'terrier-like shake.'

findings.source_passage: I'm not the least bit afraid of you. And as I've said before, and shall doubtless say again, little Tuppence can look after herself, thank you!
findings.source_locator: Tuppence's post-departure monologue on the street
findings.why_it_matters: The full self-referential formula — 'as I've said before, and shall doubtless say again' — is a recurring voice-signature for Tuppence's self-aware bravado; the draft cuts it, losing the ironic meta-commentary on her own catchphrase.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore: 'I'm not the least bit afraid of you. And as I've said before, and shall doubtless say again, little Tuppence can look after herself, thank you!'

findings.source_passage: Disdaining the spiky pen and thick, black treacle which a beneficent Government had provided, Tuppence drew out Tommy's pencil which she had retained
findings.source_locator: Post office scene, before the telegram text
findings.why_it_matters: This satirical aside — 'thick, black treacle which a beneficent Government had provided' — is a textually distinctive comic register marker; the draft drops it entirely and simply notes she wrote 'with Tommy's pencil,' erasing the period irony.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore at least the phrase about the government pen/treacle to preserve Christie's satirical voice in this passage.

findings.source_passage: The last five words took Tuppence's fancy mightily, especially after a meagre breakfast and a supper of buns the night before. Her present part was of the adventuress rather than the adventurous order
findings.source_locator: After Whittington says 'How much do you want?'
findings.why_it_matters: The narrator's distinction between 'adventuress' and 'adventurous' is an interpretive and voice-establishing comment on the moral ambiguity Tuppence is embracing; the draft replaces it with only 'Those last five words sang to her,' losing both the irony and the thematic framing.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore: 'Her present part was of the adventuress rather than the adventurous order, but she did not deny its possibilities,' along with the motivation of the meagre breakfast.

findings.source_passage: To arrive before the time would look over-eager. So Tuppence decided to walk to the end of the street and back again.
findings.source_locator: Opening of the second morning scene, before Tuppence enters the building
findings.why_it_matters: This brief internal-logic beat is characteristic of Christie's light free-indirect rendering of Tuppence's social calculations; its omission slightly thins the characterisation without significant damage.
findings.suggested_fix: Consider adding the walk-to-end-of-street beat to preserve Tuppence's self-conscious social reasoning.

summary: The draft preserves the plot and most key dialogue but systematically flattens Christie's voice in four signature passages — the terrier simile, Tuppence's self-referential catchphrase, the satirical government-pen aside, and the narratorially crucial 'adventuress rather than adventurous' distinction — producing three or more medium-severity findings that collectively constitute a voice-erasure requiring regeneration.
